title: Byte-map tokenizer sampling proposal
content:
Summary:

Short proposal for a low-overhead "byte-map" prefilter to reduce CPU work on tiny requests by avoiding full tokenization in the common-case. The idea: do an extremely cheap scan (bitmap lookup) over the first N bytes to determine whether expensive boundary-detection/tokenizer state machine needs to run. If the probe indicates a simple path (e.g., ASCII-only, no special punctuation that would create expensive multi-byte decode or escape handling), we fast-path to the minimal parse (or even send raw bytes to model input). Otherwise, run the full tokenizer.

Why we need this:
- Tiny/PL-to-LLM requests (<= 64 bytes) dominate tail-latency samples and are extremely sensitive to fixed per-request CPU overhead from parsing/tokenizing.
- Current profiler traces show ~40-120us spent in tokenizer/parse for many small requests at p50/p95 depending on GC and worker handoffs.
- Batching/kv-cache help token compute; parse overhead remains per-request. We need micro-optimizations that are cheap and deterministic.

Guiding constraints:
- Probe must be sub-microsecond on hot path (target < 0.5us per request in optimized C), and safe to run from per-request hot threads without adding syscalls.
- Must not change semantics for requests that require full tokenization; fallbacks must be exact (no token drift).
- Integrate with threadpool model and cooperative yield (avoid extra GIL holds in Python path).
- Incremental deploy: probe off by default; opt in per-route for experiments.

Design sketch - byte-map probe:
1) Precompute a 256-bit bitmap (4 x u64) where each bit indicates a byte value that is "tokenizer-simple" (e.g., ASCII letters, digits, space, newline, common punctuation that tokenizer treats as token separators in cheap cases).
2) For a request payload (first N bytes, e.g., 64), load 8 bytes at a time and compute an OR-mask over indexes -> test against the bitmap using vectorized ops or a small LUT. Early-exit after encountering a byte that maps to "complex" set.
3) If the first N bytes are all in the simple-set, skip the full tokenizer and use minimal whitespace-split path or a precomputed canonical tokenization (safe path: run tokenizer with a tiny C fast path that only handles ASCII simple set). Otherwise, run full tokenizer.

Why byte-map vs token-boundary-sampling:
- Boundary-based heuristics require scanning for token boundary characters and maintaining parser state; they can still hit slow code for escapes, unicode, or percent-encoding.
- Byte-map is data-driven: cheap bit tests and early exit; avoids branch explosion for the common ascii-only tiny-request case.
- Works well when distribution has a long tail of ascii-only or plain english prompts.

Implementation notes / options:
- C-extension vs Rust FFI: implement the probe as a tiny C routine that performs unaligned 64-bit loads and table lookups; expose a single PyCapsule to Python to avoid GIL in the scan if we call from Python worker. Alternatively, implement in Rust with cbindgen for safer memory handling.
- Vectorized path: if we have SSE/AVX available in dedicated hosts, use 16/32-byte loads and a per-byte table (PSHUFB style) for faster checks. Fallbacks for cloud hosted autotuned builds.
- Fallback correctness: if probe indicates simple and we take the fast-path, we must either run the tokenizer in a canonical deterministic C fast path (guaranteed to match full tokenizer outputs) or use the full tokenizer to generate tokens and cache result for reuse. The probe itself cannot be allowed to silently change tokenization output.

Pseudo algorithm (C-like):
uint64_t bitmap[4]; // precomputed
bool simple_scan(const uint8_t *p, size_t L) {
  size_t i = 0;
  for (; i + 8 <= L; i += 8) {
    uint64_t v = unaligned_load_u64(p + i);
    if (!check_8bytes_simple(v, bitmap)) return false;
  }
  for (; i < L; ++i) {
    if (!byte_is_simple_map(p[i], bitmap)) return false;
  }
  return true;
}

where check_8bytes_simple does 8 byte-index table-lookups packed into few ops. Microbench later.

Experiment plan:
- Goal metrics: per-request CPU us for parse/tokenize p50/p95/p99; per-request total latency tail; additional cycles from probe.
- Baseline: current release build perf traces on small-req workload (100RPS synthetic, seqLen 32 tokens, variety of prompts). Collect perf, flamegraphs, eBPF stackcounts, and microprofiler samples.
- Implement prototype in C (non-AVX) as a local module. Measure per-request overhead for probe (cold, warm). Target <0.8us including Py->C minimal call.
- Compare three flows: (A) baseline full tokenizer, (B) probe + C fast-path tokenizer, (C) probe + skip-tokenizer (only when semantics allow).
- Workloads: tiny plaintext (ascii), tiny with emojis/multibyte, header-like json, short html, run with 8, 24, 64 concurrent worker threads.
- Collect metrics: wall ms latency histogram, cpu us breakdown (parse/tokenize/other), syscall counts, context switches, GC cycles.

Commands and data collection (notes):
- Flamegraph perf: perf record -F 99 -g -- ./server-binary --load-test --qps 200 --payload-file tiny-ascii.txt
- eBPF sampling: sudo ./scripts/bpf-capture -p $PID -d 30 -o /tmp/bpf-tiny-ascii.folded
- Python microprofiler snapshots with per-request tags (use our microprofiler in-case of pyshim).

Rough expected numbers (very approximate):
- Current tiny-req tokenization: 40-120us (varies with GC and copy overhead)
- Probe runtime: naive Python call: 2-4us (too slow); C entry: ~0.4-0.7us; vectorized assembly: ~0.15-0.25us per 64B window.
- Effective savings: if 60% of requests fast-path, we can reduce total parse CPU by ~30-50% for small-req mix. Tail effects depend on GC and worker handoffs.

Integration with threadpool and Python overhead:
- We need to avoid touching the GIL for probes called on hot path. Expose PyCapsule that can be called with GIL released, or call probe from native worker thread before entering Python-managed code. For cases where request routing already involves Rust/C++ worker threads, run the probe there and pass a flag to Python runtime.
- When probe leads to C fast-path tokenizer that also avoids allocations (stack-based tiny buffer), we can further avoid GC impacts.

Safety checks and telemetry:
- Add instrumentation that records: probe_result (simple/complex), probe_latency_us, tokenization_latency_us, token_count, fallback_count. Use low-cardinality tags per route.
- For first rollout, enable verbose logging for a small sample (1% traffic) that records the input prefix and why a request fell back (multibyte, punctuation, escape). Ensure we redact PII.

Open questions / risk list:
- How to build and ship C-extension in Redwood Hosted with multi-arch (AVX/no-AVX, arm64)? Work with release-engineering for wheel building or provide a small WASM fallback?
- Are there prompt families that intentionally rely on tokenizer quirks such that our fast-path would change model behavior? Need deterministic equivalence tests (eval suites) before enabling for customer traffic.
- Interaction with our shared tokenizer caches (prefix caches): if we skip full tokenization, how do we map to cached entries? Might need to materialize canonical tokens for caching.

Next steps (short-term):
- Spike: implement probe C-extension prototype (non-AVX) and measure raw call latency from Python. Owner: Marco. ETA: 1 week.
- Add microbench harness and synthetic corpuses (ascii, emoji, escaped-json). Owner: Sofia. ETA: 1 week.
- Create deterministic token equivalence tests for the fast-path for a set of 10K short prompts sampled from production (redacted). Owner: Aisha + Solutions Eng. ETA: 2 weeks.
- Perf run: baseline vs probe vs probe+fast-tokenize on dedicated instance type (g6dn.xlarge or our internal 80GB GPU proxy) and collect flamegraphs. Owner: Devon. ETA: 2 weeks.

Notes to self / scratch fragments:
- Idea: keep a per-route sample of 500 inputs and continuously check false-positive rate (i.e., probe says simple but canonical tokenizer yields complex).
- Consider combining with prefix KV caching: if a route has heavy prefix reuse, the probe may short-circuit most requests into cache hits which further reduces tokenization.
- Implementation trick: store the 256-bit map as four u64 constants aligned in code; allows two memory reads + bit ops. Avoid indirect loads.
- Danger: branch predictor thrash if distribution changes rapidly; prefer branchless checks where possible.

TODO (short):
- [ ] Prototype C probe skeleton + Python binding.
- [ ] Run microbench for call overhead in three runtimes (dev box, CI container, dedicated infra).
- [ ] Add telemetry scaffolding to ingestion path.
- [ ] Write Canary rollout plan + kill switch.

References / inspiration:
- Fast microparsers (SAX-like) and ascii-only fastpaths in web-servers.
- Prior tokenizer microcache work in repo (see token-boundary-caching).

Bottom line: a cheap byte-map prefilter looks promising to reduce per-request CPU for small, ascii-heavy prompts. Risk is operational complexity (build/runtime) and semantic drift; those can be mitigated via deterministic equivalence tests and staged rollout.
